prompt: What is the C4 model for documenting a software architecture?
completion:
# The C4 Model – A Quick‑Start Guide

> **C4** is an acronym for **C**ontext, **C**ontainers, **C**omponents, **C**ode.  
> It is a pragmatic, diagram‑centric approach to describing software architecture, created by **Simon Brown**.  
> The goal is to provide clear, consistent, and lightweight visuals that can be understood by both technical and non‑technical stakeholders.

---

## 1. The Four Layers

| Layer | What it shows | Typical audience | Diagram size |
|-------|---------------|------------------|--------------|
| **Context** | The big‑picture of the system: *what* it does, *who* interacts with it, and *what external systems* it talks to. | Product owners, executives, new hires | One diagram |
| **Containers** | The high‑level runtime components that run the system (web app, API, database, mobile app, micro‑service, etc.). Shows *technology choices* and *deployment boundaries*. | Architects, DevOps, stakeholders | One diagram |
| **Components** | The logical decomposition inside a container: modules, services, libraries, etc. Focuses on *responsibilities* and *inter‑component relationships*. | Developers, lead architects | One diagram per container |
| **Code** | (Optional) A diagram of the actual classes, packages, or files that implement a component. Shows *internal structure* and *dependencies*. | Developers, code reviewers | One diagram per component |

> **Why “Code”?**  
> The “Code” level is rarely shown in architectural documentation because the other three layers already capture the essential decisions. It is kept for *very detailed* situations or for tools that generate code‑level diagrams automatically.

---

## 2. Visual Notation (the “C4” style)

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| **Rounded rectangle** | Container (an application, service, database, etc.) | `[[WebApp]]` |
| **Rectangular box** | Component inside a container | `[[AuthService]]` |
| **Arrow** | Data flow / dependency | `User -> WebApp` |
| **Cloud icon** | External system or actor | `<<Cloud>>` |
| **Stick figure** | Human user or system actor | `<<User>>` |

> These shapes are intentionally simple; they can be drawn by hand or generated by tools such as Structurizr, PlantUML, Lucidchart, draw.io, or even hand‑sketched on a whiteboard.

---

## 3. A Minimal Example

### 3.1 Context Diagram

```plantuml
@startuml
!define C4P https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master
!includeurl C4P/C4_Deployment.puml
!includeurl C4P/C4_Context.puml

Person(customer, "Customer")
System_Boundary(s1, "E‑Commerce Platform") {
  System(system, "Online Store")
  System_Ext(db, "Product Catalog API")
}
Rel(customer, system, "Orders")
Rel(system, db, "Queries")
@enduml
```

**What we see**

- A *customer* (human actor) uses the **Online Store** system.
- The system talks to an external **Product Catalog API**.

---

### 3.2 Container Diagram

```plantuml
@startuml
!includeurl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master/C4_Container.puml

System_Boundary(s1, "Online Store") {
  Container(webApp, "Web Front‑End", "React + Node.js", "Handles UI")
  Container(api, "REST API", "Spring Boot", "Business logic")
  Container(db, "Order DB", "PostgreSQL", "Persistence")
}
Rel(webApp, api, "HTTPS")
Rel(api, db, "JDBC")
@enduml
```

**Key points**

- *Technology choices* are explicit (`React`, `Spring Boot`, `PostgreSQL`).
- *Deployment boundaries* are clear.

---

### 3.3 Component Diagram (for the REST API)

```plantuml
@startuml
!includeurl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master/C4_Component.puml

Container(api, "REST API") {
  Component(orderSvc, "Order Service", "Handles order lifecycle")
  Component(productSvc, "Product Service", "Reads product catalog")
  Component(paymentSvc, "Payment Service", "Integrates with Stripe")
}
Rel(orderSvc, productSvc, "Reads")
Rel(orderSvc, paymentSvc, "Creates payment")
@enduml
```

---

## 4. How to Use the C4 Model

| Step | What to do | Tips |
|------|------------|------|
| **Define scope** | Pick a system that needs a high‑level architecture. | Start with the *Context* to keep the picture manageable. |
| **Create one diagram per level** | Keep each diagram focused on one abstraction level. | Avoid clutter – show only the entities that matter. |
| **Document decisions** | Pair diagrams with Architecture Decision Records (ADR) that explain *why* certain containers/components were chosen. | ADRs are linked in the diagram or in your documentation hub. |
| **Iterate** | Update diagrams as architecture evolves; keep them live docs. | Use automated generation (e.g., Structurizr) to keep them in sync. |
| **Share with stakeholders** | Publish the diagrams in Confluence, GitHub Wiki, or as part of a design deck. | Use the *Context* diagram for non‑technical audiences. |
| **Tool‑friendly** | Choose a tool that fits your workflow. | Structurizr (web + DSL), PlantUML (text + CI), draw.io (drag‑and‑drop). |

---

## 5. Why C4 Rocks

| Feature | Why It Matters |
|---------|----------------|
| **Hierarchical clarity** | You can zoom from a high‑level overview down to code‑level details. |
| **Unified language** | All architects, developers, and product owners speak the same “C4” language. |
| **Lightweight & agile** | Diagrams are quick to produce, easy to read, and inexpensive to maintain. |
| **Tool‑agnostic** | Works with plain text (PlantUML), DSL (Structurizr), or GUI (draw.io). |
| **Focus on responsibilities** | Encourages thinking in terms of *what each component does* rather than *how it is implemented*. |

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| **Over‑engineering diagrams** | Limit each diagram to one level. Keep complexity to the *Component* layer. |
| **Static only** | Pair diagrams with ADRs, run‑time metrics, and documentation on failure modes. |
| **Missing stakeholders** | Show *actors* in the Context diagram; they anchor the system. |
| **Ignoring security** | Add a *Security Context* diagram or annotate arrows with “TLS”, “OAuth”, etc. |

---

## 7. Quick Reference – PlantUML Syntax

```plantuml
@startuml
!includeurl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plantuml-stdlib/C4-PlantUML/master/C4_Context.puml

'--- Context ----------------------------------------------------
Person(user, "User")
System_Boundary(s1, "My System") {
  System(system, "Main App")
}
Rel(user, system, "Uses")

'--- Containers --------------------------------------------------
System_Boundary(s2, "My System") {
  Container(web, "Web App", "React", "Serve UI")
  Container(api, "API", "Spring Boot", "Business logic")
  Container(db, "DB", "PostgreSQL", "Persist data")
}
Rel(web, api, "HTTPS")
Rel(api, db, "JDBC")

'--- Components --------------------------------------------------
Container(api) {
  Component(order, "Order Service", "Handles orders")
  Component(payment, "Payment Service", "Handles payments")
}
Rel(order, payment, "Calls")
@enduml
```

> Replace the placeholders (`My System`, `Main App`, etc.) with your real names. The syntax is deliberately short, so you can type it quickly and regenerate diagrams on the fly.

---

## 8. Resources

| Resource | What it offers |
|----------|----------------|
| **C4 Model official site** | https://c4model.com |
| **Structurizr** | Web service & DSL for C4 diagrams, integrates with ADRs. |
| **PlantUML C4 extension** | https://plantuml.com/c4 |
| **Simon Brown’s book** | *Succeeding with Architecture*, chapters on C4. |
| **GitHub example repo** | https://github.com/structurizr/structurizr-example |

---

## 9. Take‑away

- **C4 is a *set of diagram levels***, not a modeling language.  
- Use the **Context → Containers → Components** hierarchy to describe a system from the outside in.  
- Keep diagrams *simple, focused, and linked to decisions*.  
- Leverage tools that support C4 to keep diagrams live and consistent.

With this framework, you can document a software architecture that *everyone can understand*, *everyone can maintain*, and *everyone can improve*. Happy diagramming!
